function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written them so that they work out‑of‑the‑box with a typical Node JS app that listens on port 3000 (the most common default).  
If your app uses a different port or has a different entry point, just tweak the numbers or the `CMD` line accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node 18 on Alpine
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the files needed for the install step
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command – change if your entry point is different
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the latest LTS Node version.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The container only contains the production dependencies, keeping the image lean.

---

## 2. Kubernetes manifests

Create a file called `k8s.yaml` (or split into `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml` if you prefer).  
Replace `<your-registry>` with the registry you’ll push the image to (e.g. `ghcr.io/<org>` or `docker.io/<org>`).

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <your-registry>/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80          # Service port exposed inside the cluster
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service (internal only).  
> * If you want external access, change `type: LoadBalancer` or `NodePort`.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Checkout the repo
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # Set up Node.js
    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    # Install dependencies
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    # Build Docker image
    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

    # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    # Push Docker image
    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    # Optional: Tag the image as `latest` and push
    - name: Tag & push latest
      run: |
        docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Triggers on every push to `main`.  
> * Installs Node, runs tests, builds a Docker image, and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).  
> * Uses the commit SHA as the image tag – guarantees immutability.  
> * Also tags the image as `latest` for convenience.

---

## 4. Add, commit, and push

```bash
# From the root of the repo
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> Make sure you have write access to the repo and that the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret is available (it is automatically provided by GitHub Actions).

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally**  
   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome
   ```
   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

2. **Deploy to a cluster**  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
   kubectl get pods
   kubectl get svc
   ```

3. **Push to GitHub** – the workflow will automatically build and push the image.

That’s it! Once you push, the GitHub Actions pipeline will kick off, build the image, and publish it to GHCR. Your Kubernetes manifests are ready to be applied to any cluster that can pull from that registry. Happy coding!
